scene.testo: May 1945. Four weeks after Hitler's death. An American intelligence officer sits across from the man who built the German tank arm. The interrogation report is stamped secret. Somewhere in the middle, the officer asks one simple question.

What do you think of our General Patton? Heinz Guderian did not hesitate. First, he paid Patton the highest compliment one tank general can give another. Then he repeated what Hitler had said about Patton, in a room where Guderian stood beside him.

What he did not mention that day was a boast he had made to the same Americans three days earlier. A claim about how a duel between him and Patton would really have ended. First, the room and the men who sat in it.

The room belonged to a U.S. Seventh Army interrogation center. Three German generals sat at the table that day. The Americans wanted one thing from all of them. How armored warfare truly worked, as seen by the men who fought it.

The first page carried a warning. Anyone passing on the information had to reword it, so that no one could tell who said it or how it was obtained. Guderian was listed simply as a colonel general in the officer reserve.

A general without a command. Twenty years earlier, he had been a signals officer with an idea. He argued that tanks should not crawl beside the infantry. They should move together, fast, in their own divisions, linked by radio.

In 1937, he put all of it into a book titled Achtung, Panzer. Most senior German officers considered it reckless. Across the ocean, a cavalry officer named George Patton had led America's first tanks into battle in 1918.

The two men never faced each other on any battlefield. Three years after his book, Guderian got his chance to prove the idea. In May 1940, his panzer corps crossed the Meuse River at Sedan. Then it simply kept going.

Within a week, his tanks reached the English Channel. They moved so fast that his own superiors ordered a halt. In the dispute that followed, Guderian offered to resign and was relieved. Then he was told to continue.
In June, his tanks raced all the way to the Swiss border. Remember that advance. In 1944, he would throw it in Hitler's face. In Russia, his tanks helped close a huge pocket around Kiev.

Then, in the freezing winter before Moscow, he pulled his troops back without permission. At Christmas 1941, Hitler dismissed him. For more than a year, the father of the German armored force stayed at home.
In 1943, as the war turned, Hitler brought him back as inspector of armored troops. In July 1944, the day after the bomb plot against Hitler, Guderian became chief of the army general staff.

From that post, at Hitler's headquarters, he said he watched an American general do exactly what he himself had done in 1940. On the afternoon of August 1, 1944, Patton's Third Army began to move in Normandy.

The Americans had just broken through near Avranches. There was one narrow road and a single bridge to get out. Patton pushed his divisions across and let them loose across France. His rule was simple.

A good plan violently executed now is better than a perfect plan next week. German commanders called the situation crazy. They told Hitler the Americans could not be stopped. This is the moment Guderian described to the American officer.

He said he was with the Führer when Patton's attack began. According to Guderian, Hitler looked at the map and called it nothing but reckless impudence by a few tanks. Our generals, he said, could never do that.

Guderian told him that was exactly what his own tanks had done on the road to the Atlantic coast in 1940, to the Swiss border, and around the Russian pockets. A tank commander who does not lead recklessly, he told the Americans, can never succeed.

Patton did not slow down. By the last day of August, his tanks had taken Verdun. In the words of the official U.S. Army history, with little resistance. About 300 miles in a single month. Then the fuel ran out.

But by then, Guderian had noticed something else about the Americans. Something his panzers never had. Patton was not moving alone. Over each of his armored divisions flew a cover of fighter-bombers, the P-47 Thunderbolt.
They were relieved in shifts from dawn until dusk. Pilots and tank commanders spoke directly to each other by radio. A column facing a German gun did not wait for artillery. It called the aircraft.

Their commander, General Otto Weyland, sat beside Patton at his morning meeting every day. Patton later wrote that whenever armor and air worked together this way, the results were certain to be excellent.

In September, Hitler ordered a counterattack against Patton's army near a French village called Arracourt. German tanks rolled out of the morning fog. As long as the fog held, they were safe. Then the fog lifted.

In one attack, P-47s arrived and scattered the formation within 15 minutes, leaving 11 wrecked tanks behind. A German corps commander later complained that whenever the weather improved, American aircraft swooped down on his corps.

Whenever he asked for Luftwaffe support, he was told German airfields were closed by bad weather. This is what Guderian told the Americans next. The coordination between your air forces and your armor in the Lorraine campaign was astonishing.

He said he immediately put those American tactics into the curriculum of the armored troops school at Bergen. The father of blitzkrieg was now teaching his students how Patton fought. It was the highest compliment one tank general can pay another.

But it was not the whole story. Three days earlier, the same interrogation center had questioned him for another report. There, he said German tank commanders facing Patton were not allowed to use their own judgment. They had to follow Hitler's plans.
Then the report records one more sentence. Guderian believed he could have stopped General Patton in France, had he been left free to use his own strategy. He blamed Hitler. He blamed the Luftwaffe.
What he did not mention was that as chief of the army general staff, his job was the Russian front. He never commanded a single tank against Patton. It was a claim no one could ever test.

Every failure traced back to a dead man in Berlin, and none to Guderian. The American officer who wrote the report saw the game. He noted the prisoner spoke freely only because Hitler's death had released him from his oath.

He added that Guderian apparently wanted to appear anti-Nazi. So which answer was true? Perhaps both. Patton was brilliant, as Guderian told it, because he did what the Germans had done first, and he won because Hitler would not let them repeat it.

Seven months after that interview, Patton died of injuries from a car accident in Germany. Guderian was never put on trial. He spent the following years writing history for the U.S. Army, and died in 1954.

After the war, the Americans took his memory seriously and his excuses less so. His account of Patton survives in the files, a compliment and an alibi side by side, written down by the men who sat across from him.

Guderian was not the only man the Americans questioned that spring. When they asked Hitler's admiral, Karl Doenitz, why the U-boats were lost, he named a single invention. That story is on your screen now.
Subscribe for more of what the men on the other side said in their own words, and watch that next clip. The files are still there, and the questions are still worth asking.
These were men who had given orders in the hardest years of the war. Now they gave answers, in plain rooms, to officers taking notes. History keeps both the answers and the silences.

descrizione:
In May 1945, an American intelligence officer asked Heinz Guderian, the man behind German armored warfare, what he thought of General George S. Patton. His answer, recorded in a U.S. Seventh Army interrogation report, mixed high praise with a repeat of Hitler's own words about Patton's advance.

This documentary follows the history behind that answer: Guderian's tank theories, the 1940 breakthrough at Sedan, Patton's drive across France in August 1944, the P-47 air cover over Third Army, and the fighting at Arracourt.

We also look at why the report matters, and why its author doubted the prisoner's claims. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more accounts from the men who were there.
